Row keys come from the request body unvalidated (lib/system.ts:109-120 BackupPayloadSchema uses z.record(z.string(), z.array(z.record(z.any())))); sanitiseRow() (lib/system.ts:145-152) strips secret-looking VALUES only, never column NAMES. The table is allowlisted (BACKUP_TABLES, lib/system.ts:22-42) and user_id is re-stamped, but the identifiers are not validated. Neon has no RLS (db/migrations/001-core.sql:6-13).
findings.impact: Any authenticated landlord can execute arbitrary SQL in the application database. With options.on_conflict='replace' the generated statement can be turned into `insert into public.properties ("id") values ($1,$2,$3) on conflict (id) do update set "user_id" = $3`, where $3 is the attacker's own uid: the victim's property/tenant/payment/expense/maintenance/note/document row is REASSIGNED to the attacker, who can then read, edit and delete it. The 'skip' branch inserts brand-new rows owned by an arbitrary user_id. The injected value is readable back through the ordinary APIs, so this is a read primitive as well. Cross-tenant read/write of another landlord's data.
findings.fix: Validate every row key against the real column set of the target table before building SQL and never interpolate an unverified identifier. Add a per-table column allowlist plus an identifier-shape test, and apply it in all three branches (skip/replace/merge) of neonDb.insert. Example: const IDENT=/^[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*$/; const BACKUP_COLUMNS={properties:[...],...}; for (const key of Object.keys(row)) { if (!IDENT.test(key) || !BACKUP_COLUMNS[table].includes(key)) throw new Error(`Illegal column ${key}`) }. Also fix supabaseDb.insert to use the same allowlist.
findings.fix_notes: lib/backup.ts now validates every row key against a strict identifier pattern AND the table's real column list (read from information_schema, cached) before any SQL is built, on all three insert branches (skip/replace/merge). A pre-flight check in restoreBackup() rejects the WHOLE restore before writing anything. Regression test: lib/backup.security.test.ts (27 assertions).

findings.title: Tenant invite upsert uses user_id as the conflict target, so an invite can reassign another landlord's tenant-portal link
findings.evidence:
46 |   const { data, error } = await supabase
  47 |     .from("tenant_users")
  48 |     .upsert(
  49 |       {
  50 |         user_id: matched.id,
  51 |         tenant_id: tenant.id,
  52 |         invited_by: userId,
  53 |         invited_at: new Date().toISOString(),
  54 |         accepted_at: new Date().toISOString(),
  55 |       },
  56 |       { onConflict: "user_id" },
  57 |     )
  58 |     .select()
  59 |     .single()

The tenant ownership check above (lines 20-27) verifies the TENANT belongs to the caller, but nothing verifies that the invited auth account (matched.id, resolved from the body e-mail at lines 15-17 and 35-37) is not already linked to a different landlord's tenant. tenant_users.user_id is unique (supabase-setup/08-tenant-portal.sql:13, db/migrations/002-support.sql:281), so ON CONFLICT (user_id) DO UPDATE MOVES the existing row: tenant_id becomes the attacker's tenant and landlord A's tenant loses its portal user.
findings.impact: Tenant-portal link takeover between landlords. The invited account's portal resolves to landlord B's tenant instead of landlord A's, and landlord A is left with no portal user. Currently the Supabase path is protected only by the ABSENCE of an UPDATE policy on tenant_users (supabase-setup/08-tenant-portal.sql:26-56 defines select/insert/delete only), so the request errors instead of hijacking; the Neon copy of the table (db/migrations/002-support.sql:280-288) has no RLS at all, and there is no application-level check.
findings.fix: Do not use the invitee's uid as the conflict target and refuse to steal an existing link: (1) load the existing tenant_users row for matched.id; (2) if it exists and its tenants.user_id !== userId, return 409 'That account is already linked to another workspace'; (3) upsert with { onConflict: 'tenant_id' } instead of { onConflict: 'user_id' }. Keep the RLS UPDATE policy absent or add one that requires the caller to own the tenant.
findings.fix_notes: app/api/tenants/[id]/invite/route.ts now checks any existing tenant_users link for the auth account and refuses (409) when it points at a tenant the caller does not own.

findings.title: DELETE /api/tenants/[id]/invite deletes a tenant<->user link with no ownership check on the tenant
findings.evidence:
64 | export const DELETE = withAuth(async (_req, { supabase, userId }, params) => {
  65 |   // Unlink a tenant from any auth user.
  66 |   const { error } = await supabase
  67 |     .from("tenant_users")
  68 |     .delete()
  69 |     .eq("tenant_id", params.id)
  70 |   if (error) return errorResponse(error.message, 500)
  71 |   return successResponse({ ok: true })

Contrast with the POST handler in the same file (lines 20-27), which loads the tenant and checks .eq('user_id', userId). The DELETE handler never loads the tenant; `userId` is destructured and never used. The only predicate is tenant_id = params.id, which the caller fully controls.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user who learns a tenant UUID can unlink that tenant from its portal account, destroying another landlord's tenant-portal access (rent statement, landlord contact) and the invitation state. The response is {"ok": true} either way, so the attacker gets no signal and the victim cannot distinguish a deletion from a no-op. On the Supabase path the tenant_users_landlord_delete RLS policy (supabase-setup/08-tenant-portal.sql:44-51) currently filters the delete to zero rows - an accidental backstop that does not exist on Neon (db/migrations/002-support.sql:280-288).
findings.fix_notes: app/api/tenants/[id]/invite/route.ts DELETE now verifies the tenant belongs to the caller (404 otherwise) before unlinking.

findings.title: GET /api/mpesa/c2b/status/[transId] falls back to an unscoped Daraja query that discloses another workspace's payer identity
findings.impact: Cross-tenant disclosure of payer PII and payment amounts. Any authenticated landlord can call GET /api/mpesa/c2b/status/<transId> with a trans id belonging to another workspace and read back that tenant's MSISDN, legal name, amount and receipt number. A trans id is not secret: it is printed on every M-Pesa receipt and SMS, is the TransID Daraja calls back with, and is stored in c2b_transactions.raw for every workspace. The fallback is not an edge case on the Supabase path - it is the ONLY path: the Supabase writer omits user_id (app/api/mpesa/c2b/confirmation/route.ts:235-251) but the column is `user_id uuid not null` (supabase-setup/10-holy-grail.sql:92), so the insert is rejected, no c2b_transactions row is ever created, and the scoped cache lookup never matches.
findings.fix: Never fall back to a provider lookup for a transaction you do not own. If the cached row is missing, it is not the caller's: return 404. Query the cache with `where trans_id = ${transId} and user_id = ${userId}` and drop the c2bTransactionStatus(transId) fallback, or re-check ownership of the returned transaction before returning it.
findings.fix_notes: app/api/mpesa/c2b/status/[transId]/route.ts no longer falls back to an unscoped Daraja query. A transaction that is not in the caller's own rows returns 404.

c2bRegister() (lib/mpesa/daraja.ts:355-389) calls Safaricom with the PLATFORM's MPESA_CONSUMER_KEY / MPESA_CONSUMER_SECRET (lib/mpesa/daraja.ts:46-58). The schema accepts any short_code and any https:// validation_url / confirmation_url; there is no ownership check on the short code and no role check.
findings.impact: Platform-level privilege escalation from a normal landlord account. The attacker re-registers the platform's own paybill shortcode with an attacker-controlled confirmation URL, so every C2B payment customers make to the platform is confirmed to the attacker's server, leaking payer MSISDN, legal name and amount, and letting the attacker accept or reject the platform's rent collection. The platform's own callback (app/api/mpesa/c2b/confirmation/route.ts:83-213) then never runs, silently breaking reconciliation for every landlord.
findings.fix: Treat URL registration as an operator action, not a user action: require a server-side secret header (x-mpesa-admin-secret compared against MPESA_ADMIN_SECRET) and no user session, and require the short code to exist in the caller's own paybills row (.eq('number', short_code).eq('user_id', userId)). Better: delete the route and run the registration from a deploy script.
findings.fix_notes: POST /api/mpesa/c2b/register is now an operator-only action. The app has no enforced role model, so operators are named explicitly in MPESA_ADMIN_EMAILS (a comma-separated allowlist); unset means NOBODY is an operator and the route refuses to run (503). The Daraja short code is now validated as a numeric 6-10 digit Safaricom shortcode, and both callback URLs must be https. Residual risk: the allowlist content — keep it to addresses the owner controls, because Supabase sign-up is open.

findings.impact: Cross-tenant write into another landlord's property/tenant graph. Landlord B creates a tenant attached to landlord A's property (POST /api/tenants with property_id = A's id) and a forged rent_payments row pointing at landlord A's tenant (POST /api/payments with tenant_id/property_id = A's ids). Because the reconciliation candidate set is `from tenants t left join properties p ... where p.user_id = ${userId}` (app/api/mpesa/c2b/confirmation/route.ts:126-133, app/api/reconciliation/match/route.ts:40-47), B's forged tenant becomes a match candidate for A's incoming M-Pesa payments, and A's money is written into rent_payments under A's uid but against B's tenant row. The same trick works for maintenance requests, notes, documents and expenses attached to A's property.
findings.fix: Validate every foreign key against the caller's own rows before writing. Add a helper, e.g. lib/api/ownership.ts: async function assertOwned(supabase, table, id, userId) { if (!id) return; const { data } = await supabase.from(table).select('id').eq('id', id).eq('user_id', userId).maybeSingle(); if (!data) throw new HttpError(`${table} not found`, 404) }, and call assertOwned(supabase,'tenants',fields.tenant_id,userId) / assertOwned(supabase,'properties',fields.property_id,userId) in every affected handler (and payment_id against rent_payments in app/api/mpesa/stkpush/route.ts). Rejecting an unknown id with 404 also removes the oracle.
findings.fix_notes: app/api/payments/route.ts now verifies the referenced property AND tenant belong to the caller before writing (404 otherwise).

Same pattern in: app/dashboard/properties/[id]/page.tsx:29-30, app/dashboard/tenants/[id]/page.tsx:33-41, app/dashboard/documents/[id]/page.tsx:27-33, app/dashboard/maintenance/[id]/page.tsx:27-33, app/dashboard/contacts/page.tsx:22-23, app/dashboard/paybill/page.tsx:22-23, app/dashboard/damages/page.tsx:23, app/dashboard/properties/map/page.tsx:51-60.

Every API route does scope correctly (e.g. app/api/properties/[id]/route.ts:22-31, app/api/notes/[id]/route.ts:13-22). The RLS policies that cover the pages live in supabase-setup/*.sql, which the operator must paste into the Supabase SQL Editor by hand; the patch runner applies them to Neon (app/api/migrations/run/route.ts:110-143), where auth.uid() does not exist so RLS is never enabled. The architecture states Neon is the primary DB and has no RLS (db/migrations/001-core.sql:6-13).
findings.impact: Defence in depth is missing on the screens that show the most sensitive records. If the Supabase RLS policies were never applied, or the data lives on Neon, any authenticated user can read another landlord's notes, documents (identity documents, in a PUBLIC bucket - see CRYPTO-005), tenant details, maintenance records, contacts, paybills and damages simply by changing the id in the URL. The detail screens render any id, including app/dashboard/tenants/[id]/page.tsx:38-41 which returns another tenant's payment history.
findings.fix: Scope the page queries by user_id exactly like the API routes do. The browser Supabase client can filter on user_id: resolve the session with supabase.auth.getUser() and add .eq('user_id', userId) to every query (for example app/dashboard/notes/[id]/page.tsx). For list screens add .eq('user_id', userId) to the query; for team-shared views resolve the company first and filter on company_id the way app/dashboard/company/page.tsx:25-36 already does.

findings.title: Properties map counts every landlord's properties with an unscoped query on the Neon primary database
findings.impact: select count(*) from public.properties on Neon has no user_id predicate and Neon has no RLS, so every authenticated user sees the platform-wide property count in the 'Total properties' tile, and the derived 'Need geocoding' and 'Coverage' figures are computed against the global total instead of the caller's portfolio. Low sensitivity (an aggregate count, no PII) but a genuine cross-tenant leak that is guaranteed to work on the Neon path, with no backstop. The Supabase fallback at lines 157-159 is equally unscoped.
findings.fix: Scope the count to the caller: `select count(*)::int as n from public.properties where user_id = ${userId}`, and add .eq('user_id', userId) to the Supabase fallback query at lines 157-159.

The paywall gate reads the subscription_status RPC (lib/supabase/middleware.ts:103-115), whose semantics are defined in supabase-setup/14-subscriptions.sql:112-179: a row with status='trialing' and trial_ends_at IS NULL skips the 'trial expired' branch (lines 137-147) and falls through to the final block (lines 162-176), which returns is_active = true with days_left = 0 - active forever. The reactivate branch writes trial_ends_at back as current.trial_ends_at, which is NULL for any row created by the checkout path (app/api/subscription/checkout-status/route.ts:57-68 never sets it).
findings.impact: Self-service bypass of the 14-day trial and the KES 2,490/month paywall, and of the plan_code tier. PATCH {"cancel":true} followed by PATCH {"reactivate":true} on a lapsed subscription with trial_ends_at = NULL yields a permanently 'active' subscription, so the middleware stops redirecting to /dashboard/billing; trial_ends_at is NULL for any row created by the checkout path (app/api/subscription/checkout-status/route.ts:57-68) and the reactivate branch itself nulls it whenever it lands on 'active' (app/api/subscription/route.ts:124). Two further gaps soften the same gate: a row with status='active' whose current_period_end has passed is still reported is_active=true (supabase-setup/14-subscriptions.sql:162-176 uses current_period_end only for days_left), and PATCH {"plan":"pro"} sets the plan tier with no payment. The user_id predicate is correctly applied, so there is no cross-tenant impact - hence MEDIUM rather than HIGH.
findings.fix: The subscription row must not be client-writable. Reject the free plan switch and the free reactivation: PATCH {plan} -> 402 'Plan changes require a payment'; PATCH {reactivate:true} -> 402 'Reactivation requires a confirmed payment', and let only the verified M-Pesa/Stripe callbacks (app/api/subscription/checkout-status/route.ts:55-79, app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts:26-44) set status='active'. Also harden the RPC so a 'trialing' row with trial_ends_at IS NULL is treated as expired (supabase-setup/14-subscriptions.sql:137).

findings.title: Open redirect: the post-authentication 'next' sanitiser accepts a backslash-prefixed protocol-relative URL
findings.impact: Open redirect on the authentication surface, reachable without any secret: sending a signed-in user https://<app>/auth/login?next=/%5Cevil.com makes the server redirect to the attacker's domain. The link looks like a PropDesk URL, so it is a clean credential-phishing primitive (and a way to launder a malicious link through the app's own trusted domain). The same value works on /auth/callback?code=...&next=/\evil.com.

findings.title: M-Pesa C2B callbacks trust the client-controllable x-forwarded-for header and the IP allowlist fails open when unset
findings.impact: If the route is reachable, an attacker can POST a forged Daraja payload (BusinessShortCode = a real paybill number, attacker-chosen TransAmount and MSISDN) and the handler writes a 'paid' rent payment for that workspace (app/api/mpesa/c2b/confirmation/route.ts:184-194) - forged rent collection and receipts that were never paid. Honest status: today the route is unreachable anonymously because the middleware 401s every /api/** path except the three in isExternalApi (lib/supabase/middleware.ts:55-58,82-87) - which also means the LEGITIMATE Safaricom callback is broken. The control actually protecting the route is the blanket 401, not the IP check, so this must be fixed together with the middleware allowlist.
findings.fix: Authenticate the callback with a shared secret the way app/api/mpesa/callback/route.ts:29-36 already does (timingSafeEqual on x-mpesa-callback-secret), keep the IP allowlist as a second factor, fail closed (lib/mpesa/daraja.ts:270-272: if (list.length === 0) return false - never 'allow all'), and read the client IP from a header the platform overwrites. Then add the two C2B paths to the middleware's public-API allowlist so the legitimate callback works.

findings.title: The middleware matcher excludes every path ending in .js/.css/etc., so dynamic API routes skip the middleware's 401 entirely
findings.evidence:
13 | export const config = {
  14 |   matcher: [
  15 |     /*
  16 |      * Run middleware on every path except:
  17 |      *  - _next/static  (static chunks)
  18 |      *  - _next/image   (image optimizer)
  19 |      *  - favicon / image / asset files
  20 |      */
  21 |     "/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|.*\\.(?:svg|png|jpg|jpeg|gif|webp|ico|css|js)$).*)",
  22 |   ],
  23 | }

The negative lookahead excludes any path whose last segment ends in one of those extensions. Next.js dynamic segments match dots, so GET /api/tenants/<uuid>.js is routed to app/api/tenants/[id]/route.ts with params.id = '<uuid>.js', and the path never matches the matcher, so updateSession() never runs and the 401 at lib/supabase/middleware.ts:82-87 is never produced.

LOW today: every dynamic API route that touches tenant data also uses withAuth (server-side getUser), so no data leaks through this bypass. The routes reachable this way (app/api/blog/[slug], app/api/docs/[slug], app/api/features/[slug], app/api/customers/[slug], app/api/templates/[id]/**) return static marketing content.

Other shapes checked and NOT exploitable: trailing slash (pathname still starts with /api/), double slash (Next.js answers 308 for repeated slashes, node_modules/next/dist/server/base-server.js:576-581), encoded slash, upper case (App Router matching is case-sensitive -> 404), query strings.
findings.impact: The middleware is not a reliable authorisation layer for dynamic API routes. The day an unauthenticated-by-design route with a dynamic segment is added, or withAuth is dropped from one of them, the '.js' suffix is a one-character authentication bypass. The middleware's coverage claims are wrong today even though nothing leaks yet.
findings.fix: Narrow the exclusion to the static-asset directories instead of a file-extension pattern, e.g. matcher: ['/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|robots.txt|sitemap.xml).*)'], or list the API surface explicitly first: matcher: ['/api/:path*', '/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|.*\.(?:svg|png|jpg|jpeg|gif|webp|ico|css|js)$).*)'].

findings.title: The middleware skips all enforcement when the Supabase env vars are missing
findings.impact: If NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL or NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY is missing (mis-set env, a preview deployment without secrets, a build without NEXT_PUBLIC_* inlined) the middleware returns immediately: no 401 for /api/**, no redirect for /dashboard/**, and no email-verification gate (lib/supabase/middleware.ts:90-94). The withAuth routes still 401 on their own getUser() call, so tenant data stays protected; what is lost is the middleware's own layer - anonymous access to the routes that have no withAuth wrapper, and the unverified-email redirect.

findings.title: The tenant-invite route calls the Supabase admin API on the anon client (broken today, latent user-enumeration primitive)
findings.evidence:
29 |   // Resolve the auth user id from email via the admin API
  30 |   // (we need the service-role key for this)
  31 |   const { data: userList, error: lookupErr } = await supabase.auth.admin.listUsers()
  32 |   if (lookupErr) {
  33 |     return errorResponse("Cannot look up users — service role required", 500)
  34 |   }
  35 |   const matched = (userList?.users || []).find(
  36 |     (u: any) => (u.email || "").toLowerCase() === email,
  37 |   )

`supabase` here is the anon-key server client from lib/supabase/server.ts:33-53 (NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY). The Supabase admin API requires the service-role key, so listUsers() fails with 403 and the route always returns 500 - the invite feature is non-functional as written.
findings.impact: None today (the call fails). If it is 'fixed' naively by swapping in createServiceClient() (lib/supabase/service.ts:15-25) it becomes a full enumeration of every user account on the platform (e-mail address, id, created-at), reachable by any authenticated landlord who can post an e-mail address, with no rate limit.
findings.fix: Do not enumerate users. Resolve the invitee through a mechanism that does not read the user table - have the tenant sign up with the e-mail and claim the link with a one-time token, or use the Supabase admin INVITE api (which creates the user rather than listing them). If enumeration is unavoidable, gate it on a service-role client AND an admin secret and rate-limit it.
